newsitem.title: FRANCE: Giscard d'Estaing wants Spain, Italy in Euro.
newsitem.headline: Giscard d'Estaing wants Spain, Italy in Euro.

text.p: Former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing says European leaders might be able to grant "conditional acceptance" to Italy and Spain so they can be in the first wave of countries in Europe's single currency in 1999.

"It is highly important Italy and Spain be members of the first wave of countries launching the euro," the International Herald Tribune newspaper quoted him Thursday as saying, "because their participation will give a truly European flavour."
"If we are just restricted to those countries centred around the Rhine, it will simply look like an enlargement of the Deutsche mark zone and not a genuinely European endeavor."

Giscard said the Maastricht treaty on monetary union was clear in specifying countries must meet deficit and other criteria before 1999 to join the single currency and stressed Italy and Spain could only be admitted if they met them.
But he said European leaders who will meet in early 1998 to decide which countries qualify could agree on a solution to pave the way for Spain and Italy to be part of the first wave.
He said "it was only for practical purposes that we have to decide in the spring of 1998 on who joins and that it is in order to create a European central bank."

"The difficulty will be those countries that in 1997 will not meet the criteria but that obviously will meet them by January 1999," he said. "The trend will have to be very clear, and the numbers solid but at that point we may have a solution."
He urged discussions among government chiefs in the spring of 1998 "about the trend and then a decision in principle could be made" about which countries could join.
"It could be a conditional acceptance," he said, "with the implementation delayed until they meet the criteria and that could be January 1999 or a few months later."

Giscard d'Estaing, who triggered a row last November when he called for a weaker French currency, publicly breaking a taboo on questioning France's decade-old strong franc policy, said he told President Jacques Chirac before he made his call.
Chirac's spokeswoman confirmed on Thursday he told the president last summer "about his views on monetary questions. But it's clear the proposals of the former president only engage himself."
Giscard d'Estaing had urged that the franc depreciate against the dollar which has since appreciated strongly.

He said the dollar-franc level was now "appropriate" and that, "We are in a very good target zone." When he made his call last November, the dollar was worth about five francs. On Thursday, the franc stood at 5.6750 to the dollar.

Giscard d'Estaing, wading again into the debate over French monetary issues, urged a "more active" policy that would not be afraid of cutting short-term interest rates to German levels to spur growth.

French rates are currently slightly above German rates. He said there was "no reason for French interest rates at present to be higher than German rates. I think French interest rates can and should be reduced to the same range."
In the interview, he also lamented a lack of political leadership throughout the European Union.
The exception, he said, was German Chancellor Helmut Kohl... "who has a definitive vision of the future of Europe. Today's European political leaders "are addressing the problems as they come."
"They are all embattled...and the public perceives this."
